system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2135-11-23 15:04:00 to 2135-11-24 18:36:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with a complex medical history including end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease with prior CABG and stents, peripheral vascular disease, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for sudden-onset sub-sternal chest pain that occurred during a dialysis session. The pain was consistent with his known angina and resolved with nitroglycerin and morphine. Serial troponins remained stable without rise, and CK levels trended downward, indicating no acute myocardial infarction. EKG showed new T-wave flattening in leads V2-V5. The patient was observed for over 24 hours, remained pain-free, and completed dialysis. Management included continuation of cardiac medications, discontinuation of Nexium due to potential interaction with Plavix, and transition to ranitidine. He was discharged home with instructions to follow up promptly with his cardiologist, monitor weight daily, and continue wound care for a chronic leg ulcer. No stress testing was performed due to low likelihood of changing management.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

overlying the right atrium and ventricle.  Moderate cardiomegaly is stable. 
There is no focal pulmonary consolidation or edema.  There is persistent
bibasilar atelectasis.  A loculated small right pleural effusion is unchanged,
and tracks into the right minor fissure.  The osseous structures are
demineralized, with stable degenerative changes in the thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION:  Stable cardiomegaly and small right effusion.

microbiology.comments: Due to mixed bacterial types (>=3) an abbreviated workup is performed; P.aeruginosa, S.aureus and beta strep. are reported if present. Susceptibility will be performed on P.aeruginosa and S.aureus if sparse growth or greater.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with chest pain this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I woke up at 4 a.m. with tightness in my chest and felt nauseous. I took two nitroglycerin pills and vomited, which helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And then you went to dialysis, but the pain came back there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right when I arrived. They sent me straight to the ER. I didn’t have any sweating or shortness of breath this time, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your vitals are stable—blood pressure around 140/60, heart rate in the 60s. We’ve given you some morphine and more nitroglycerin for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s much better now. But I’m worried—could this be a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking that. We’ve drawn blood to look at your cardiac enzymes, like troponin. The first one came back slightly elevated but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Slightly elevated? Does that mean damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. With your history—three-vessel disease, bypass surgery, stents—your baseline can be a bit higher. We’ll repeat the test to see if it’s rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had chest pain during dialysis before. It’s not new, but this time I felt sicker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. The nausea and vomiting make this episode more concerning. We want to rule out unstable angina or a small heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a nuclear stress test tomorrow to see how your heart is getting blood. It will help us decide if you need a catheterization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last time I had chest pain, they said my enzymes were flat. Is it the same thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, yes. But we can’t assume. This time, we’re being cautious because of the nausea. We also noticed some fluid at the base of your right lung on the chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fluid? Is that from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. With your history of heart failure and kidney disease, fluid can build up. We’ll manage that with your next dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to go tomorrow. Will I still do it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve coordinated with dialysis. They’ll remove extra fluid carefully, especially after your stress test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my leg ulcers—should I keep up with the wound care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ve arranged for you to see podiatry tomorrow after your stress test. They’ll assess the ulcers on your right tibia and left toe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been using the cream they gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We also checked a wound swab today just to make sure there’s no infection. Preliminary report shows no anaerobes, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it’s not infected. It’s been slow to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. For now, rest and let the team manage your fluids and heart symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have your stress test results. The good news is—no reversible defects. That means no active ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no blockage that needs fixing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. There’s a fixed defect in the inferior wall, which matches your old heart damage. But nothing new that would benefit from a stent or surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So why the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s due to inadequate collateral blood flow, especially during stress like dialysis. We’re adjusting your meds to help prevent it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes are we making?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your metoprolol to 37.5 mg twice daily—that’s one and a half pills. It helps reduce the heart’s workload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m already on a lot of heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re simplifying one: stopping the isosorbide dinitrate and switching to isosorbide mononitrate once a day. It’s longer-acting and easier to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll take one pill instead of three?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. One 60 mg and one 30 mg pill daily. We’ll send both with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? My PCP just changed it last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your new regimen: 12 units of glargine at bedtime and lispro before meals. Just monitor your sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds, call your doctor. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow up with my cardiologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within a week. Also, keep your podiatry appointments and continue wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already saw them yesterday. They cleaned the ulcers and said they’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. You’re stable and pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I was really worried this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your tests show no heart damage, and we’ve made good adjustments. Keep taking your nitroglycerin if chest pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. A nurse will go over your updated medication list before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure all my doctors have the same list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very important. We’ll also send a summary to your PCP and cardiologist.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with a complex history including end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease with prior CABG and stents, peripheral vascular disease, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for sudden-onset chest tightness associated with nausea and vomiting. The pain began at home and recurred during a dialysis session, prompting ER evaluation. Initial troponin levels were stable, and a nuclear stress test showed no reversible ischemia, indicating no acute coronary event. Management focused on optimizing anti-anginal therapy, including increasing metoprolol and switching from isosorbide dinitrate to once-daily isosorbide mononitrate. Fluid overload was noted on chest imaging and managed with dialysis. The patient also received podiatry care for chronic lower extremity ulcers. He remained stable, pain-free, and was discharged home with medication changes, weight monitoring instructions, and follow-up plans.
